¿Cómo se resuelve la ecuación de Laplace: How is the Laplace equation solved by relaxation?
Se divide la caja en una malla y cada pu: The box is divided into a grid and each interior point is replaced by the mean of its four neighbours, V(i,j) = ¼[V(i+1,j) + V(i−1,j) + V(i,j+1) + V(i,j−1)], repeating until the change is smaller than the tolerance. Jacobi uses the values of the previous iteration, Gauss-Seidel the most recent ones, and SOR speeds them up with a factor between 1 and 2.
¿Se puede comprobar el resultado a mano?: Can the result be checked by hand?
Sí, en casos simétricos. Si un borde de: Yes, in symmetric cases. If one edge of a square box is at 100 V and the other three at 0 V, the potential at the centre is the mean of the four edges, 25 V, and the numerical solution should approach that value.
Fija el potencial de los cuatro bordes d: Set the potential of the four edges of a box (and, if you want, of an electrode inside it) and watch how the potential is distributed by relaxation: colour map, equipotential lines and electric field. Click on the map to place the probe.

En una región sin cargas el potencial el: In a region without charges the electric potential satisfies $∇² V = 0$. Its solutions are harmonic functions: they have no maxima or minima in the interior, so the highest and lowest potentials are always on the boundary. And the solution is completely fixed once the potential on the whole boundary is known (uniqueness theorem).
El potencial en un punto es la media de: The potential at a point is the mean of its values over a circle around it. On a square grid this means that each node equals the mean of its four neighbours:
Se empieza con un reparto cualquiera y s: You start with any distribution and replace each node by the mean of its neighbours until it stops changing. Jacobi computes all nodes with the values of the previous sweep; Gauss-Seidel already uses the new values and takes half as long; SOR overshoots the mean value a little (over-relaxation, with $1 < ω < 2$) and for a grid of $N$ cells needs of the order of $N$ sweeps instead of $N^2$. Compare the three with the method selector.
Una vez conocido el potencial, el campo: Once the potential is known, the field is its gradient with the sign changed, $E = −∇V$: it is perpendicular to the equipotentials and points where the potential decreases. On a conductor (the electrode) the field leaves perpendicular to its surface.
With charge in the region, $∇² V = −ρ/ε_0$. Relaxation only changes in the source term: $V_{i,j} = {V_{i+1,j} + V_{i−1,j} + V_{i,j+1} + V_{i,j−1}}/4 + {ρ h^2}/{4 ε_0}$. If the charge is uniform between two grounded plates, $V(x) = {ρ x (a − x)}/{2 ε_0}$.
En un borde aislante el campo no lo atra: At an insulating edge the field does not cross it ($∂V/∂n = 0$) and it is solved with a mirror node. The charge of each conductor comes from Gauss's flux, $Q' = ε_0 ∮ E_n dl$, and the capacitance per metre of two conductors is $C' = Q'/ΔV$, which also equals $2W'/ΔV^2$ with the energy $W' = ½ ε_0 ∫ E^2 dA$.
Para una caja de lados $a$ y $b$ con un: For a box of sides $a$ and $b$ with a single edge (the top one) at $V_0$ and the others at 0, the exact solution is a Fourier series, with $n$ odd:
Los otros bordes aportan lo mismo girado: The other edges contribute the same rotated, and by superposition it holds for any combination. The tool uses it to measure the grid error when there is no electrode.
